newsitem.title: PERU: Peru June GDP growth seen over 7pct year over year.
newsitem.headline: Peru June GDP growth seen over 7pct year over year.

text.p: Peru's gross domestic product (GDP) in June is likely show seven percent growth from the same month a year ago, led by the construction, agricultural and fishing sectors, analysts said Thursday.

Earlier this week the financial daily Gestion quoted economy ministry sources as saying the June figure would show eight percent year-over-year growth. The government is due to release its official June GDP figure in the next few days.
One analyst, Pablo Secada of Santander Investment, said the construction sector's robust performance in June may have lifted the overall GDP figure as high as nine percent.

High cement sales and government investment in the country's road network indicated the construction sector could register year-on-year growth of up to 15 percent, said Aldo Quintana, an analyst at the Interfip brokerage.
A solid June GDP figure would stand as further evidence that Peru's economy has regained its footing after a prolonged slowdown last year.
Analysts now forecast 1997 GDP growth to exceed the government's estimate of 5.0 percent. The economy expanded by 2.6 percent last year.
The government's latest published figures show cumulative GDP growth for the first five months of 1997 at 7.2 percent, compared with 1.1 percent growth in the same period last year.

In June, the agriculture sector also put in a robust performance, in part because farm operators are beginning to reap the rewards of an emphasis on long-term investments, according ot Alvaro Valencia, an analyst at brokerage Prisma.

The Argos brokerage, which estimated an overall year-on- year economic growth of 7.2 percent in June, mentioned the fishing sector as another strong performer in the month, despite concerns over the destructive climatic pheneomenon known as El Nino, which is forming off Peru's Pacific coast.
The weather pattern, which affects Peru every two to five years, hampers fishing and agricultural output because of unseasonal temperatures along the coast and in the Andes.

Still, analysts said the phenomenon would not noticeably affect Peru until next year. Even then the government might be able to limit its impact because early warnings have enabled it enough to adapt its policies, they added.

The government, which has set up a ministerial commission and an emergency fund to deal with the problems related to El Nino, has held steady with its official estimate of five percent annual economic growth during the next few years.
